fieldWork.label: The Blueprint of the Post Road

lesson.text: Every system tells two stories: what it does, and where the data goes.

A DATA FLOW DIAGRAM (DFD) maps the movement of data through a system so both engineers and lawyers can see the same picture. Four symbols, that's the whole alphabet — you already drew them on the Post Road.

THE FOUR SYMBOLS

▭ EXTERNAL ENTITY (square) — a person, system, or store OUTSIDE your control that interacts with your system. Villagers and couriers; patients and doctors. These mark your system's BOUNDARY and are where privacy risk enters and exits.

◯ PROCESS (circle) — an activity INSIDE the system that acts on data: transforms, routes, or redirects it. Bram's sorting desk; a hospital management system.

═ DATA STORE (parallel lines) — where data rests, briefly or forever. The overnight vault; a patient database. Usually where the sensitive material accumulates.

→ DATA FLOW (arrow) — the movement of data from source to destination. The arrows ARE the privacy story: follow them to see who touches what.

The power of a DFD is that it makes the invisible legible. You cannot protect a flow you cannot see — and most breaches happen on a flow nobody drew. When you mapped the Post Road and the rogue arrow to the Bandit Camp appeared, you were doing THREAT MODELING: comparing the system as documented against the system as run.

DEPTH LAYERS

A DFD can zoom. LAYER 0 (a "context diagram") shows the whole system as a single process with its external entities — the view for a boardroom. LAYER 1 breaks that process into its major sub-processes. LAYERS 2-3 drill deeper still. Match the depth to the risk: a high-risk system earns a deeper map. Draw only as deep as the decision in front of you requires.

Two privacy lenses ride on top of the diagram. PURPOSE LIMITATION asks, at every arrow: does this destination need everything in this flow, or only part? (The sorting desk needed the address, not the contents.) And DATA MINIMISATION asks, at every store: must this rest here at all? A DFD turns both questions from abstract principles into things you can point at.
Below is the Village Post Road, drawn properly at last. Read it like a Ranger.

nodes.label: Villagers
nodes.roleExplain: Villagers are an EXTERNAL ENTITY — outside the system, sending mail in. They don't process or store anything themselves.

nodes.label: Cipher Desk
nodes.roleExplain: The Cipher Desk is a PROCESS — it seals contents before they reach the sorting desk. It doesn't hold anything long-term.

nodes.label: Sorting Desk
nodes.roleExplain: The Sorting Desk is a PROCESS — it routes mail by address. It doesn't store anything overnight, and needs only the address, not the contents.

nodes.label: Overnight Vault
nodes.roleExplain: The Overnight Vault is a DATA STORE — sorted bundles rest here till dawn. This is where accumulated data, and accumulated risk, sits.

nodes.label: Couriers
nodes.roleExplain: Couriers are an EXTERNAL ENTITY — outside the system, carrying mail onward. They don't process or store anything themselves.

nodes.label: Bandit Camp
nodes.roleExplain: The Bandit Camp is an unauthorized EXTERNAL ENTITY receiving a flow it was never meant to see — that IS the information disclosure threat.

arrows.roleExplain: This arrow carries villagers' mail into the Cipher Desk — a normal, authorized flow.

arrows.label: contents-sealed
arrows.roleExplain: This arrow carries contents-sealed mail from the Cipher Desk to the Sorting Desk — the desk gets the address, not the contents.
This arrow moves sorted bundles into the Overnight Vault — a normal, authorized flow.
This arrow shows couriers drawing bundles from the vault at dawn — a normal, authorized flow.
This dashed arrow is the rogue flow — mail leaving the system through an entity that was never authorized to receive it.

questions.prompt: Click the DATA STORE in this system.
questions.explain: Parallel lines = where data rests. The vault holds sorted mail overnight, so it's where accumulated data — and risk — sits.

questions.prompt: Click an EXTERNAL ENTITY that the system does NOT control but must account for.
questions.explain: Squares outside the boundary; you can't govern them, but your privacy analysis must include them.

questions.prompt: Click the PROCESS whose job requires ONLY the address, not the contents.
questions.explain: Purpose limitation — it routes by address; giving it the contents would violate "need to know." This is why the Cipher Desk sits before it.

questions.prompt: Click the element that represents an INFORMATION DISCLOSURE threat.
questions.explain: An unauthorized external entity receiving a flow = information disclosure; the whole reason you encrypt the contents upstream.

questions.prompt: The Council wants a single-picture summary for a village meeting — no internal detail. Which DEPTH LAYER do you draw?
explain: Exactly — the context diagram shows the system as one process with its external entities. No internals exposed, the boardroom view.
Too deep. Layer 2 already exposes internal sub-processes the Council doesn't need for a summary.
Far too deep. The full diagram is a working document, not a summary — it would bury the one picture they asked for.
